notes.meaning: Just as a few dead flies cause a jar of sweet perfume to rot and smell bad, so a single foolish act can ruin an honorable reputation. A good name takes years of wisdom to build, but it can be destroyed in an unguarded moment. Small sins carry great power to spoil much good.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Early church father Jerome understood the dead flies as evil thoughts stirred up by the devil, which spoil the sweet fragrance of a believer's holy life.

notes.meaning: The right hand is a symbol of skill, readiness, and favor, while the left points to weakness and error. A wise man's heart directs him toward what is good and sensible, keeping him on guard. A fool's inner thoughts lead him into clumsy, misguided, and sinful behavior.

A fool cannot hide his lack of understanding from those around him. Even in his simple, daily routine, such as walking down a public road, his foolish behavior reveals what he is. His words and actions openly put his foolishness on display for everyone to see.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: The Latin Vulgate translates the verse to mean that the fool in his arrogance assumes every person he meets on the road is a fool.

notes.meaning: If a ruler or superior becomes angry with you, do not quit your position in haste or resentment. Staying at your post with patience and a calm spirit can quiet great anger. Humility and gentle submission prevent greater conflict and bring healing to serious offenses.

The teacher notes a widespread injustice he has observed in earthly life. It is a serious mistake that flows directly from those in supreme authority. When rulers exercise poor judgment in how they govern, disorder ripples through the entire community.

Rulers often promote incompetent and foolish people to high offices of dignity and power. Meanwhile, those who are rich in wisdom, noble character, and good judgment are left in lowly positions. This inversion of order produces great misery for the nation.

In the ancient world, riding on horseback was a privilege reserved for persons of royal honor. The teacher laments seeing unworthy, servile men elevated to high honor while true nobles are forced to walk on foot like servants. Human governments frequently turn God's natural order upside down.

A person who digs a ditch or trap for others is very likely to fall into it himself. Likewise, anyone who tears down a stone boundary wall risks being bitten by a snake hidden in the cracks. Those who maliciously attack others or break established protections end up bringing harm upon themselves.

Even necessary, honest labor comes with built-in risks. A worker quarrying heavy stone blocks can be crushed by them, and a person splitting logs can be hurt by flying chips or axe blades. Wisdom teaches us that any significant enterprise requires caution and care.

Working with a dull, unsharpened axe requires a person to expend far more brute strength and achieve poorer results. Taking the time to sharpen the blade beforehand makes the work smooth, safe, and successful. Wisdom and thoughtful preparation always accomplish far more than raw muscle.

A snake charmer gains nothing from his trade if the serpent strikes before he has whispered his charm. In a similar way, a slanderer or babbling person does damage before anyone can restrain him. Wisdom must be applied at the right moment to prevent disaster.

A wise man speaks with kindness, grace, and good sense, winning the favor and goodwill of those who hear him. A fool, on the other hand, speaks recklessly and brings about his own destruction. His own lips become a snare that ruins his life and reputation.

A fool's speech begins with silly, empty thoughts and rapidly gets worse as he continues. By the time he finishes, his words have escalated into harmful, uncontrollable madness. An undisciplined tongue easily moves from foolish talk to destructive malice.

A fool talks endlessly, boasting and making bold claims about things he cannot possibly know. No human being knows what the future holds, nor can anyone reveal what will happen after he dies. Truly wise people speak with humility because only God controls what is to come.

Fools exhaust themselves with heavy labor that accomplishes nothing because they lack basic common sense. Not knowing the way to the city was an everyday saying for failing to grasp what was plain and obvious to everyone. Without practical wisdom, even the simplest duties of life become wearisome struggles.

A country faces disaster when its king is childish, immature, and incapable of sound judgment. The tragedy is deepened when high officials spend their mornings feasting and drinking instead of handling the nation's business. Starting the day in self-indulgence leads to neglected duties and civil decay.

A nation is blessed when its king possesses noble character, wisdom, and moral maturity. Under such leadership, officials eat at proper times for bodily strength and service, rather than for drunken revelry. Self-control and dedication in leaders provide peace and security for their people.

When a homeowner is lazy and refuses to make timely repairs, the roof beams slowly sag and rot until rain pours through the ceiling. In the same way, lazy rulers who neglect their responsibilities allow the structure of the whole nation to fall into ruin. Diligence is necessary to keep families and governments from collapsing.

Banquets are held for laughter and wine brings cheer to earthly life, but money is the practical resource that pays for both and supplies daily necessities. In this fallen world, money serves as the common tool to buy food, clothing, and shelter. The proverb realistically notes money's usefulness in earthly affairs without declaring it can satisfy the soul.

One should never curse a ruler, even in the privacy of one's thoughts or within a locked bedroom. Treasonous words have a way of being discovered and reported, as if carried on the wings of a bird. God also hears every secret whisper, reminding believers to guard their speech and respect authority.
